segments.text: American Fork City Council — Budget Workshop — February 10–11, 2022:

City Administrator David Bunker identified the police/courts building as a project with a critical timeline. He said the Police Department had completely outgrown its space and explained the tradeoffs involved in extending the courts’ lease, reclaiming the upper floors, or pursuing a city justice court.

entities.speaker: Anna Montoya
entities.remark-context: Police contract costs and retention funding

segments.text: Finance Director Anna Montoya reported that the Cedar Hills contract’s 2% annual increase did not cover rising costs, that public-safety spending had increased while other departments’ shares declined, and that maintaining competitive public-safety compensation required approximately $730,000. She presented property-tax options to fund that need and roads.

entities.speaker: Robert E. Shelton
entities.remark-context: Property-tax option after public-safety retention analysis

segments.text: After staff identified public-safety employee retention as the largest reason for a proposed tax increase, Council Member Robert Shelton supported the lower of the two increase options discussed, followed by annual adjustments.

entities.speaker: Clark P. Taylor
entities.remark-context: Property-tax option after public-safety retention analysis

segments.text: After staff identified public-safety employee retention as the largest reason for a proposed tax increase, Council Member Clark Taylor said the lower option was already consumed by existing needs and favored considering the higher option, followed by annual adjustments.

entities.label: Police/courts building capacity and lease options

segments.text: The city identified the Police Department’s lack of space as a critical facility decision and considered how the courts’ lease, rental revenue, and possible justice-court costs affected available police space.
Relevant passage from the official meeting minutes:

There are four projects with critical timelines:
• Police/Courts. Unfortunately, they have more officers packed into the police department than they ever thought they would, and they have completely outgrown the building. Currently, the courts have the second and third floor of the building and the contract will expire the end of September. However, there is an option for a 5-year extension that if they choose to. The city will need to re-evaluate the price per square foot and get back with the courts. If the courts were to move, they would lose the rent revenue, but the rent revenue does not cover the bond payments for a new building. It was beneficial to the police department to have the courts in American Fork, but the legal department has been looking into the possibility of having our own Justice Court. Ms. Egner explained she was unable to find any city that came out ahead with a justice court when they factor in the prosecutors.

entities.label: Cedar Hills contract costs, public-safety retention, and tax options

segments.text: The workshop connected the economics of contracted police services, public-safety employee retention, and proposed property-tax increases.
Relevant passages from the official meeting minutes:

There was a discussion on the Cedar Hills contract and the annual increase of 2%. It was noted that does not cover the increases, but they do pay additional funds when go over the agreed upon number of calls.

Ms. Montoya went over the general fund expenditures by department. Public safety has increased while every other department has gone down.

Ms. Montoya asked why they would increase the property tax rate. There were several reasons, but the biggest reasons were public safety employee retention; the amount increased for public safety to stay competitive was $730,000. The city was short for what was needed for road improvement; they have allocated $2.5 million a year but the needs were significantly higher. She wanted to show the tax rate scenario with the outcomes of a pegged rate, .01 increase, .025 increase, and .05 increase based on an assessed value increase of 5%. She explained if they pegged the tax rate, the increase would be approximately $22 per year per home with a total revenue increase of $221,094. For each .01 increase, the revenue brough in would be approximately $320,650.

The council discussed the options presented regarding the property tax. The city needed to look at our needs, regardless of what the school district does. Council Member Shelton felt the .25% rate increase and pegging thereafter was the best option. Council Member Taylor thought the .25% increase was already eaten up with the needs and felt they may need to choose the .5% option with pegging thereafter. It was noted the citizen survey was encouraging with the comments that they would be okay with an increase if it went towards roads.

Ms. Montoya stated they can update the schedule when they get more tax rate information in June. With truth in taxation, they would have to hold a public hearing where people may show up to make public comment; if the city were to double the rate, a lot of people will comment. It was felt the city can justify the increase. When the rate is pegged, the higher the valuation then the property taxes would be higher; if they have a double digit increase in fair market value, they will have a much larger increase. If the council opts to peg the tax rate, they will have to go through truth in taxation every year and could make a decision at that time.

Ms. Montoya went over the truth in taxation milestones. If they decide to do this, the city will need to put in the tentative budget the increased property tax. As part of the budget process, they will have meetings with time for the public to provide input. There was the discussion on pegging the tax rate and bringing it up every year or whether to have a huge bump one year and not look at it for a few years. Staff would prepare an analysis on pegging the tax rates. The council also stressed the need to get information out to the public, specifically showing what the funds will be spent on.
